source.version: Working paper, The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, dated January 27, 2024 (p. 1). The document itself shows no SSRN number; the search record gives DOI 10.2139/ssrn.4708466.
source.title_on_document: Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance

paper_design_summary: The authors prompt GPT-4 with 35 prompting strategies to generate pools of new-product ideas for college students (under USD 50), usually 10 sessions of 100 ideas per strategy. They score each pool's diversity as the mean pairwise cosine similarity of Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings and compare the pools with each other and with one existing pool of 100 ideas written by Wharton MBA students (the pool used in Girotra et al. 2023). No person receives AI help; a separate analysis generates about 1,200 ideas per session with the base and Chain-of-Thought prompts to estimate idea exhaustion and the number of unique ideas.

studies.label: GPT-4 idea pools versus a pool of Wharton MBA student ideas (cosine similarity, Table 2)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned to people. The authors generate GPT-4 idea pools under 35 prompts and compare them with an existing pool of human ideas.
assignment.quote: As a baseline for comparison, we use a pool consisting of 100 randomly chosen ideas generated by Wharton MBA students. This is the same pool of ideas used as in Girotra et al 2023.
assignment.locator: p. 5, section 'Prompting Strategies for Innovation and Brainstorming'

arms.name: Group of Students
arms.description: Pool of 100 randomly chosen ideas generated by Wharton MBA students, aggregated from multiple students working individually (p. 5). Appendix D lists its size as 10x100 (p. 20), which differs from the 100 ideas stated on p. 5.

arms.name: GPT-4 Base Prompt
arms.description: GPT-4 (gpt4-0314) prompted with the base prompt; 10 sessions x 100 ideas (pp. 5, 8-9; Appendix D).

arms.name: GPT-4 Chain of Thought (gpt4-1106-preview)
arms.description: Three-step prompt: list 100 short titles, make them bolder and more different, then write descriptions; 10x100 ideas (pp. 6, 12; Appendix A, p. 18; Appendix D, p. 20).

arms.name: Other GPT-4 prompting strategies
arms.description: The remaining strategies in Table 2: personas (Steve Jobs, Sam Altman, Elon Musk, creative entrepreneur), special techniques (tipping, emotional appeals, threats), HBR and Stanford design-thinking articles, previous top ideas, cosine information, hybrid brainstorming, and two Girotra et al. GPT-4 pools.

participants.exclusions: Not applicable to the student pool. For Chain of Thought in the exhaustion analysis, runs where the model skipped the second step were removed (about 15% of runs, p. 12).
participants.who: Wharton MBA students whose ideas form the human comparison pool; the paper does not say how many students contributed.
participants.country: United States (Wharton School); not stated explicitly for the students
participants.quote: It is important to note that students were not tasked with generating 100 ideas at once, but instead the pool is an aggregation of ideas from multiple students.
participants.locator: p. 5, section 'Prompting Strategies for Innovation and Brainstorming'

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 (gpt4-0314, temperature 0.7, top P 1.0); gpt4-1106-preview for Chain of Thought and the exhaustion analysis
ai_tool.how_used: GPT-4 generates the ideas itself under each prompt; no human uses the AI.

task.description: Generate ideas for a new physical consumer product for college students in the United States, retail price under about USD 50, each idea a named paragraph of 40-80 words.

outcomes.name: Mean within-pool cosine similarity of ideas (higher = less diverse)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Average cosine similarity between all ideas in a pool, computed per pool and then averaged over the pools of a strategy; Google's Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings (p. 9). Table 2 reports one number per strategy. Figure 2 shows density plots for selected strategies.

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity: Base Prompt 0.377 vs Group of Students 0.243 (higher similarity = less diverse). Pool differences tested by bootstrapping and permutation testing, 'p-values below 0.01', stated for pools in general, not for this pair.

Cosine similarity: Chain Of Thought (gpt4-1106-preview) 0.255 vs Group of Students 0.243. Text: 'Cosine similarity for ideas generated by groups of humans is around 0.243 compared to 0.255 - 0.432 for GPT-4 generated ideas.'

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity within a pool of ideas
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of ideas within each pool of 100 (within-pool comparison); averaged over the 10 pools of each GPT-4 strategy. The student pool is one pool of 100 ideas per p. 5 (Appendix D lists 10x100).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Bootstrapping and permutation testing; the paper states p-values below 0.01 in general and that differences between pools of 1000 ideas become significant at ~0.01; no standard errors or pair-specific tests are printed.
diversity_detail.notes: Figure 2 legend (p. 10) prints Creative Entrepreneur 0.347 and Brainstorming 0.396, while Table 2 (p. 11) prints Creative Entrepreneur 0.348 and Hybrid Brainstorming 0.393. Appendix D (p. 20) also lists a programmatic 'Lowest Cosine Add' pool at 0.144.

studies.label: Comparison of 35 GPT-4 prompting strategies and exhaustion analysis (model only)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Prompting strategy for GPT-4 idea generation; no people involved.
assignment.quote: In all strategies but hybrid brainstorming we generate a set of 100 ideas in a single GPT session using a specific prompt. In total, for each strategy, we generate 10x100 ideas over 10 sessions
assignment.locator: p. 5, section 'Prompting Strategies for Innovation and Brainstorming'

participants.who: No human participants; GPT-4 output only.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4 (gpt4-0314; gpt4-1106-preview for Chain of Thought and the exhaustion analysis)
ai_tool.how_used: GPT-4 generates ideas under different prompts; the exhaustion analysis generates about 1,200 ideas per session in 30-idea increments, 5 runs per prompt (p. 9).

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Girotra, Meincke, Terwiesch, and Ulrich (2023), 'Ideas are dimes a dozen: Large language models for idea generation in innovation' (SSRN 4526071): the student idea pool and the two 'Girota et al.' GPT-4 pools come from that paper.
sample_overlap.quote: As a baseline for comparison, we use a pool consisting of 100 randomly chosen ideas generated by Wharton MBA students. This is the same pool of ideas used as in Girotra et al 2023.
sample_overlap.locator: p. 5; Table 2 (p. 11) rows 'Girota et al. Baseline GPT-4' and 'Girota et al. Seeded GPT-4'

company_involvement.description: No company involvement stated; the authors are at the Wharton School and use the OpenAI GPT-4 API.

eligibility.reason: No person is assigned to AI assistance and the paper has no human participants of its own. GPT-4 idea pools are compared with each other (model only) and with an existing pool of 100 Wharton MBA student ideas reused from Girotra et al. (2023), whose number of contributing students is not stated (p. 5). The AI-versus-human diversity comparison (Table 2, p. 11) qualifies only as ai_vs_human context.

one_line_finding: GPT-4 idea pools are less diverse than a pool of Wharton MBA student ideas (mean cosine similarity 0.377 for the base prompt and 0.255 for Chain of Thought vs 0.243 for students), and prompting changes GPT-4 diversity across 0.255-0.432 (p. 11, Table 2; p. 3).
open_questions: Whether a paper whose main analysis is model-only, with one reused human idea pool as a benchmark, belongs in ai_vs_human context or in the screening report's model-only exclusions.
The size of the student pool: p. 5 says 100 ideas, Appendix D (p. 20) lists 'Student Ideas' as 10x100.
notes: Model-only results (S2), recorded here rather than as outcomes: estimated opportunity space about 3700 ideas for the base prompt (13.8% repetitive) vs about 4700 for Chain of Thought (11.7%) (p. 13); in the exhaustion analysis the Chain of Thought advantage in cosine similarity persists to about 750 ideas and is strongest between 100 and 500 ideas (p. 12, Figure 3 on p. 13); between-pool overlap is small (Figure 4, p. 14). Steve Jobs persona 0.368 vs base 0.377; HBR article 0.387 (p. 3; Table 2). The paper's limitations note that the 'team human' pool aggregates individuals' ideas and is likely more diverse than any individual or team could produce (p. 15).
